title: In orbit, a drop of water can circle a charged knitting needle like a tiny moon

cover.alt: A pale blue knitting needle floating against a dark background aboard the space station, with a tiny water droplet just above it.

body: In 2012, aboard the International Space Station, astronaut Don Pettit charged knitting needles by rubbing them with paper, then released charged water droplets near them from a syringe. Electric attraction pulls each droplet towards the needle, while its sideways speed carries it past, so some droplets loop round and round, much as gravity and speed keep a moon in orbit. On Earth the drops would simply fall; aboard the station they are in free fall along with everything else, so the weak electric force is enough to steer them. NASA says a simulation that included air drag matched the orbits he filmed.

slides.alt: A blue knitting needle lies across a dark background. A tiny bright water droplet swings down beneath it, round the tip, back over the top and down again, looping around the needle.
slides.caption: Space station, 2012: a tiny water droplet loops around Don Pettit's charged knitting needle, passing under it, round the tip and back over the top.

slides.prompt: Pettit needed electrically charged knitting needles. How did he charge them aboard the space station?
slides.detail: Rubbing transfers electric charge between materials, the same static you get from a balloon rubbed on a jumper.

slides.heading: How a droplet ends up in orbit

steps.label: Rubbing with paper charges the needle
A syringe releases charged water droplets
Electric attraction pulls a drop inwards
Its sideways speed carries it round

left.label: A moon
left.text: Gravity pulls it towards its planet; its sideways speed keeps it from falling in.

right.label: A droplet
right.text: Electric attraction pulls it towards the needle; its sideways speed keeps it circling.

slides.question: Why can a weak electric force steer the drops aboard the station, but not on Earth?
options: Everything there is in free fall
There is no air in the station
slides.explanation: The station and everything in it are falling around Earth together, so nothing presses the drops downwards. On Earth they would drop to the floor long before completing an orbit.
